conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here to make sure you’re getting the support you deserve as you settle into life with your new baby. I know this chapter can feel like a whirlwind of joy, exhaustion, and everything in-between.

We’re going to use a quick, well-trusted questionnaire called the **EPDS**—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—to check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. It’s simply a way for us to shine a light on any depressive or anxious symptoms that sometimes tag along after delivery, and it includes a question about self-harm so we can keep you safe. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me otherwise, and there’s no right or wrong answer—just your honest experience.

We’ll walk through ten gentle questions together. I’ll re-phrase each one in everyday language so it feels like a conversation, not a quiz. Ready to start?

First, thinking about the past week:  
**Have you still been able to look forward to things you normally enjoy, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?**

I... I mean, I still try to go through the motions. I used to love putting on music and baking while I sang along, or meeting my best friend for coffee. Now I’ll put the baby in the sling and half-heartedly stir a muffin mix, but it feels flat—like I’m watching myself do it instead of actually enjoying it. Same with the coffee dates: I go, I smile, but the happy flutter I used to get just isn’t really there. So yeah, most things feel kind of gray lately.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Mostly just the middle option, I guess. I do laugh sometimes—like when the baby lets out a huge burp and my husband and I can’t help but crack up—but it doesn’t come as easily or feel as good as it used to. A lot of the time I’m too tired or tense to find the humor in anything.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to tell myself I should be excited about little things—like when my sister offers to come over so I can take a walk, or when we planned that tiny backyard picnic. But when the moment actually arrives, it’s like someone turned the volume way down on the happy part. I still go through with stuff, partly because I feel guilty if I don’t, but the looking-forward feeling is mostly gone. So I’d say “not often” fits me better.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that sounds like me. If the baby’s fussy, I automatically think it’s because I ate something “wrong” or didn’t hold him long enough. Yesterday he wouldn’t nap and I kept replaying every little thing I did, convinced I’d messed up his routine. My head tells me babies just have off days, but the guilty voice jumps in first.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much yes. Even when everything’s calm—baby’s sleeping, the house is quiet—I’ll suddenly feel this knot in my chest that something bad’s about to happen. I’ll check that he’s breathing like five times, or worry the formula isn’t the right temperature, or imagine him rolling over when I’m not looking. I know it’s unlikely, but I can’t shake the “what-ifs.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s not every day, but every so often I’ll be feeding him in the rocking chair and out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get a full breath. Nothing triggered it—no loud noise, no bad news—just this sudden wave of “something awful is about to happen and I can’t protect him.” It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

A lot of the time, honestly. It feels like the minute I finish one feeding, the laundry pile is staring at me, the dishes are overflowing, and I can’t remember whether I’ve eaten anything besides a granola bar. Some days I manage to chip away at it, but more often I just sit there with the baby on my chest thinking, “How is everyone else doing this?” I feel like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… most nights I finally get him down by ten, and then I lie there staring at the ceiling with my mind racing—going over everything I think I did wrong or imagining scary “what-ifs.” I’ll finally drift off around one or two, but if he makes the tiniest grunt I’m instantly wide-awake again. I’m exhausted but sleep just won’t come—or stay—for more than a couple hours at a time.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes, that’s been me most days this week. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a gray cloud hanging over everything. Little tasks feel huge, and even when my husband tries to cheer me up, the sadness just sits there. I’ll find myself tearing up while folding onesies, thinking, “Is this all I’m supposed to feel now?”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried three, maybe four times this week. Once was when I couldn’t get him to latch and I felt like I was starving my own baby. Another time the microwave beeped and I just burst into tears—no real reason, just this wave of hopeless came over me. The tears come pretty easily lately.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, I haven’t had thoughts like that. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of my baby.

I hear how heavy life has felt since your baby arrived-how activities you once loved now seem gray, how the days blur into a cycle of worry, tears, and exhaustion. You are working so hard to be the parent you want to be, yet you're facing persistent sadness, nightly racing thoughts, and episodes of sudden panic that leave you shaky and convinced something bad is about to happen. Your honesty about feeling overwhelmed and crying over "nothing" shows the depth of strain you're carrying, and it makes sense that you're wondering whether others manage better than you.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter only occasionally and notes it "doesn't come as easily or feel as good as it used to," matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes marked reduction in anticipatory enjoyment; "the looking-forward feeling is mostly gone" aligns with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive self-blame ('automatically think it's because I ate something wrong') and rumination ('kept replaying every little thing'), indicating 'most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, uncontrollable worries despite objective safety, matching "Yes, very often".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes episodic panic symptoms occurring "sometimes" without triggers, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive overwhelm, inability to manage daily tasks, and feeling unable to cope 'a lot of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing thoughts, waking multiple times and sleeping only a couple hours total, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness "most days," waking heavy, tasks feeling huge, and crying—clearly matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes triggered by minor stressors, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** With an EPDS of 23, well above the ≥14 threshold, and high scores on items reflecting <sym>depressed mood</sym>, <sym>loss of enjoyment</sym>, <sym>self-blame</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>panic</sym>, and <sym>sleep disruption</sym>, findings meet screening criteria for probable <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> per <med>DSM-5</med>. The patient describes daily tearfulness, <quote>feeling heavy</quote>, <quote>volume turned down on the happy part</quote>, nightly intrusive worries, and episodes of racing heart and breathlessness without clear triggers, all indicating significant functional impairment and distress. She denies self-harm thoughts, so immediate safety concern is low, yet the symptom burden warrants urgent clinical review. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full evaluation and treatment planning
2. Discuss evidence-based options such as <med>CBT</med>, support groups, and consider <med>antidepressant medication</med> if indicated
3. Encourage 15-20 min daily outdoor walks and acceptance of help with chores to reduce overload
4. Plan a consistent bedtime routine: dim lights, hand baby to partner/friend for one nightly bottle if possible, and limit screen time after feeds
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress once treatment starts
6. Provide 24-h crisis line numbers and reinforce calling if mood worsens or panic spikes
7. Reassure her these feelings are common, treatable, and not a reflection of her abilities as a mother
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today]

Source: Patient self-report on 10-item EPDS-style questionnaire (responses recorded above).

Symptoms/Concerns  
- Persistent low mood, sadness “most days”  
- Marked anhedonia: “volume turned down on the happy part”  
- Daily tearfulness, crying episodes with minimal precipitant  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt re infant care  
- Recurrent, intrusive “what-if” worries; nocturnal hyper-arousal  
- Episodic panic symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness) unrelated to situational triggers  
- Sleep initiation/maintenance problems linked to ruminative worry  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed, unable to “tread water”

Pattern  
Responses cluster in three domains:  
1. Depressive (Q2, Q7, Q8, Q9)  
2. Anxiety/panic (Q4, Q5)  
3. Maternal guilt/self-criticism (Q3)

Screening Significance  
- Elevated risk for major depressive episode with peripartum onset  
- Co-occurring anxiety symptoms (possible panic episodes)  
- Functional impact: impaired sleep, coping, and maternal confidence

Safety  
Denies self-harm or suicidal ideation (Q10: “No… I just want to feel better”); no further safety concern elicited in responses.

Summary  
Patient endorses multiple symptoms consistent with postpartum depression/anxiety, notable for mood, enjoyment, anxiety, and sleep impairment, without self-harm intent. Formal diagnostic assessment and follow-up recommended.
